title: CUBIC for Fast Long-Distance Networks
summary: CUBIC is a TCP congestion control variant that differs from standard TCP only in the sender's algorithm. It uses a cubic function rather than a linear one to grow its window, improving scalability and stability on fast, long-distance networks. It was replaced by RFC 9438.

eli5.summary: Instead of speeding up at a steady pace, it speeds up in a curve: fast at first, slowly near the limit it last remembers.

questions: how does cubic congestion control work
why is cubic better for long-distance networks
subtitle: A TCP congestion control variant optimized for fast, long-distance networks.

tldr.problem: Standard TCP grows its sending window too slowly in networks with high bandwidth and long delays (large bandwidth-delay product). This leaves capacity unused and degrades performance on fast, long-distance links.
tldr.mechanism: CUBIC replaces TCP's linear window growth with a cubic function. It grows the window concavely (conservative near the previous peak) then convexly (probing for new capacity), and it uses a higher multiplicative decrease factor (0.7 instead of 0.5) to reduce aggressive convergence.
tldr.outcome: CUBIC achieves better utilization of high-capacity links while remaining fair to standard TCP in conventional networks. It has been the default TCP variant in Linux since adoption from its predecessor BIC-TCP. RFC 8312 was superseded by RFC 9438.

today: RFC 8312 is an informational document describing CUBIC, which has been widely deployed as the default TCP congestion control in Linux. It was superseded by RFC 9438, which provides updated specifications and analysis.

sections.title: The Problem with Standard TCP
sections.content:
TCP's original congestion control algorithm (AIMD: Additive Increase, Multiplicative Decrease) works well on conventional networks, but struggles in fast, long-distance links with large bandwidth-delay product (BDP)—the product of link capacity and round-trip latency. When a packet loss occurs, standard TCP reduces its window and then increases it by one segment per RTT. Recovery to full capacity takes many round-trips, leaving the link underutilized.

This problem affects all Reno-style TCP variants, including TCP-Reno, TCP-NewReno, SCTP, and TFRC. CUBIC, originally proposed in research, offers a solution that has since been adopted by Linux as its default TCP congestion control and deployed globally.
sections.eli5: When a package gets lost on a slow network, TCP recovers quickly. On a fast, distant network, recovery takes too long, wasting the unused capacity.

sections.title: CUBIC Design Principles
sections.content:
CUBIC is built on four core principles. Principle 1: It uses both concave (conservative) and convex (aggressive) profiles of a cubic function to improve stability and utilization. After a loss, it conservatively grows the window toward the previous peak (concave), then continues probing for new capacity beyond that peak (convex).

Principle 2: It remains TCP-friendly in small bandwidth-delay networks by behaving like standard TCP. CUBIC adjusts its aggressiveness based on the previous window size before loss: smaller windows (small BDP networks) grow less aggressively. Principle 3: It achieves fairness across flows with different RTTs by maintaining a constant window increase rate. This gives flows linear throughput ratio proportional to inverse RTT ratio, an improvement over standard TCP's quadratic ratio in some conditions. Principle 4: It uses a multiplicative decrease factor of 0.7 (compared to 0.5 in standard TCP) to balance scalability and convergence.
sections.eli5: CUBIC has four design rules: use a curved increase, play nicely with standard TCP, treat different speeds fairly, and be careful when reducing the window.

sections.title: The Window Increase Algorithm
sections.content:
CUBIC increases its congestion window using the equation W_cubic(t) = C*(t-K)^3 + W_max, where t is elapsed time since the last congestion event, W_max is the window size before the loss, C is a constant (set to 0.4), and K is calculated to reach W_max at the inflection point without further losses.

CUBIC operates in three regions. In the TCP-friendly region, the cubic function grows slower than standard TCP, so CUBIC follows standard TCP's window size to ensure compatibility. In the concave region (window below W_max), CUBIC grows conservatively, maintaining high utilization near the previous saturation point. In the convex region (window above W_max), CUBIC probes very slowly for additional available bandwidth, since network conditions may have changed.

When a loss occurs, CUBIC reduces the window by multiplying by 0.7 and updates W_max. For fast convergence when flows join or leave the network, CUBIC has a heuristic: if the new W_max is less than a remembered previous peak, it reduces W_max further to release bandwidth faster to newcomers.
sections.eli5: CUBIC tracks three regions of growth: first it copies standard TCP, then it carefully grows back to its memory of the peak, then it very slowly probes beyond that peak.

sections.title: Fairness and Compatibility
sections.content:
CUBIC was designed to be fair to standard TCP. In networks where standard TCP performs well (short RTT, small bandwidth), CUBIC behaves similarly and achieves comparable window sizes. Tables in the RFC show that with loss rates from 10^-2 to 10^-8 and an RTT of 0.01 seconds, CUBIC with C=0.4 achieves the same window size as standard TCP at loss rates up to 10^-5, outperforming HighSpeed TCP's aggressiveness.

On high-bandwidth, long-distance networks, CUBIC is significantly more aggressive than standard TCP. For 10 Gbps throughput over 0.1 second RTT, standard TCP requires a loss rate of 2.0e-10, while CUBIC requires only 2.9e-8. This allows CUBIC to use available spare capacity without starving standard TCP flows sharing the same link.

CUBIC ensures that multiple CUBIC flows with the same RTT converge to equal throughput, and flows with different RTTs have bandwidth proportional to the inverse of their RTT ratio. These fairness properties hold independent of the level of statistical multiplexing on the link.
sections.eli5: CUBIC shares fairly: it does not hog bandwidth from standard TCP, and on fast networks it grabs spare capacity that standard TCP leaves unused.

sections.title: Safety and Deployment
sections.content:
CUBIC maintains TCP's core safety mechanisms: it uses ACK clocking, performs fast recovery and retransmit like TCP-NewReno, and has the same behavior on timeouts and congestion collapse. It requires no changes to TCP receivers or routers. A CUBIC sender works correctly with standard TCP receivers, enabling incremental deployment.

CUBIC has been extensively evaluated in simulation (NS-2) and testbeds across many network scenarios. As a loss-based algorithm like standard TCP, it can fill large buffers more quickly due to its more aggressive window increase, which RFC 7567 recommends addressing through proper queue sizing and active queue management.

CUBIC does not protect against misbehaving nodes or outside attackers (deferred for future work). For application-limited flows that are not using their full congestion window, the elapsed time counter must not count idle periods, to prevent W_cubic from becoming excessively large after resumption.
sections.eli5: CUBIC is safe: it keeps the protections that make TCP reliable, works with regular TCP, and has been tested extensively. It does not defend against attackers.
